title: Leveraged ETFs Promise Bigger Returns. Here Is Why Long-Term Investors Should Weigh the Risks First
author: Leo Sun
description: Leveraged ETFs aim to double or triple returns of underlying indexes or stocks through total return swaps with banks, but they carry significant risks including daily rebalancing that erodes long-term returns, high fees, counterparty risk, and a history of failures. Over half of all leveraged ETFs have eventually failed. While the largest ones like SPXL may work for long-term S&P 500 believers, leveraged ETFs are generally considered short-term trading tools rather than buy-and-hold investments.

insights.sentiment_reasoning: Presented as the safer, traditional alternative to leveraged ETFs with low fees (0.03% expense ratio) and reliable long-term performance, recommended for buy-and-hold investors.

Acknowledged as potentially viable for long-term S&P 500 believers despite risks, with demonstrated 5-year performance of 140% vs VOO's 70%, but cautioned as a tactical tool with daily rebalancing drawbacks.
Explicitly criticized as a poor long-term investment, with shares plummeting 90% over five years as the S&P 500 reached record highs, making it unsuitable for buy-and-hold investors.
Flagged as risky for long-term investment due to being leveraged to a single stock rather than a diversified index, increasing volatility and concentration risk.

title: Why Leveraged ETFs Are Considered Among the Market's Most Speculative Products
author: Leo Sun
description: Leveraged ETFs that aim to double or triple daily gains of stocks or indexes are highly speculative and risky investment products. While they can amplify gains during bull markets, they reset daily and can compound losses during market downturns. These funds charge high fees and are better suited for short-term traders rather than long-term investors.

insights.sentiment_reasoning: Presented as a prudent long-term investment option with low fees (0.08%), offering diversified exposure to the S&P 500 without the risks associated with leveraged products.
Criticized as a speculative product that triples daily gains/losses, charges high fees (0.87%), and can compound losses during market downturns despite strong historical returns.
Mentioned as a legitimate ETF option for investors seeking exposure to higher-growth Nasdaq-100 companies without the excessive leverage and risk of leveraged ETFs.
Described as an even riskier leveraged ETF targeting a single stock, characterized as a 'greedy strategy that will inevitably backfire' for long-term investors.

title: A Leveraged Bet on the Broad Market or Big Tech: SPXL vs. QLD
author: Eric Trie
description: SPXL and QLD are leveraged ETFs offering different market exposures: SPXL provides 3x daily leverage to the S&P 500 with broader diversification, while QLD offers 2x daily leverage to the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100. SPXL has lower fees (0.87% vs 0.98%) and higher dividend yield, while QLD has larger assets under management. Both funds are designed for short-term trading rather than long-term investing due to daily leverage resets that can cause performance divergence in volatile markets.

insights.sentiment_reasoning: SPXL demonstrates stronger 5-year performance ($2,785 vs $2,128 for QLD), lower expense ratio (0.87%), higher dividend yield (0.67%), and broader market exposure across 516 holdings, making it more suitable for investors seeking diversified leveraged exposure to the broad market.

QLD offers concentrated tech exposure with 2x leverage and larger AUM ($10.75B), but underperformed SPXL over 5 years, has higher fees (0.98%), and lower yield (0.16%). It suits investors specifically targeting leveraged technology exposure but carries higher concentration risk.

title: Better High-Return ETF: SOXL vs. SPXL
author: Robert Izquierdo
description: SOXL and SPXL are both 3x leveraged ETFs designed for short-term trading. SOXL focuses exclusively on semiconductors with higher volatility and 1-year returns of 38.6%, while SPXL tracks the broader S&P 500 with more diversification and 27.2% 1-year returns. SOXL experienced a steeper 5-year drawdown of 90.51% versus SPXL's 63.84%, making SPXL relatively safer but with a slightly higher expense ratio.

insights.sentiment_reasoning: SOXL delivered strong 1-year returns of 38.6% and benefits from the hot AI/semiconductor sector. However, the positive sentiment is tempered by its extreme volatility and 90.51% max drawdown, making it suitable only for risk-tolerant traders.

SPXL offers more balanced risk-adjusted returns with 27.2% 1-year performance and significantly lower max drawdown of 63.84%. Its broader S&P 500 diversification provides better downside protection, making it the relatively safer leveraged option.

title: QLD vs. SPXL: Is Tech-Heavy Growth or S&P 500 Diversification Better for Investors?
author: Katie Brockman
description: SPXL and QLD are leveraged ETFs offering amplified exposure to major U.S. indexes with similar one-year returns (~12%) but different risk profiles. SPXL provides 3x daily S&P 500 returns with 500+ holdings for broader diversification, while QLD offers 2x daily Nasdaq-100 returns with concentrated tech exposure (55% in technology, 101 holdings). Both carry high volatility, similar max drawdowns (-63%), and daily leverage resets that can cause returns to diverge from target multiples over longer periods.

insights.sentiment_reasoning: SPXL offers broader diversification with 500+ holdings and higher leverage (3x), resulting in marginally better 5-year returns ($3,025 vs $2,417). However, it carries higher volatility risk due to 3x leverage and similar extreme drawdown risk as QLD. Suitable for investors seeking amplified S&P 500 exposure but with significant risk.

QLD provides concentrated tech exposure with 101 holdings and 2x leverage, delivering similar one-year returns to SPXL but lower 5-year returns. The heavy tech concentration (55%) offers growth potential but increases sector-specific risk. Suitable for aggressive traders seeking targeted tech exposure with high volatility.
